newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST- S.Africa Jan reserves seen at 6-mth high.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST- S.Africa Jan reserves seen at 6-mth high.

text.p: A flood of dollars into South Africa in January is expected to have boosted the gold and foreign exchange reserves to their highest levels in six months, economists said on Friday.

A Reuters consensus poll of nine economists forecast reserves would rise to 11.2 billion rand in the month from 10.3 billion rand in December. The average was drawn from a range of 10.5 to 11.5 billion rand.
Reserves were last above 11 billion rand in June 1996. The Reserve Bank will release January reserves data at 1600 GMT next Friday.
Nedcor chief economist Dennis Dykes said a sharply lower money market shortage coupled with a stronger rand pointed to a healthy increase in reserves in the month.
The money market shortage fell below the eight billion rand mark for the first time in three months on Thursday to 7.089 billion rand after having resisted traditional month-end pressure all week.

Roelf du Plooy, the Reserve Bank's assistant general manager of money and capital markets, told Reuters this week the fall in the shortage was primarily a result of banks selling dollars to the central bank.

"At the moment (commercial) banks are selling dollars back to the Reserve Bank...in quantities much larger than we expected them to," du Plooy said on Wednesday. "It is plain forex flows that is causing the shortage to come down," he said.

Money market traders also cite heavy offshore demand for domestic gilts as a reason for the declining shortage. Bond Exchange statistics show foreigners were net buyers of 1.89 billion rand's worth of bonds between January 2 and January 30.
And foreign exchange dealers have also reported heavy exporter dollar sales which have boosted the rand to its strongest level in three months.
"All these factors will provide for an increase to above 11 billion rand in January," an economist said.
Nick Barnardt, chief economist at BOE NatWest, noted however, that the inflow of foreign exchange would be offset by a considerably lower rand gold price.
The rand gold price has fallen from 1,719.83 an ounce on December 31 last year to 1,572.07 on Friday.
"The large inflows of money that occurred in January will be neutralised to a large extent by the effect of the lower gold price on the valuation of the reserves," Barnardt said.
But a London-based economist who asked not to be identified said: "Although the gold component is probably a little lower, the inflow of cash should outweigh it."
He also noted that because the rand appreciated during January, the reserves would look even better in dollar terms -- which foreigners monitor more closely -- than they did in rands.
The rand has firmed from around 4.70 at the beginning of the year to a low of 4.5525 bid on January 30.
